h: פָּרָשַׁת זָכוֹר, מַאֲמָר ה׳ Parshas Zachor — Maamar Hei

p: וְהָיָה בְּהָנִיחַ ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ לְךָ וְגוֹמֵר
"And it shall be, when Hashem your God gives you rest" etc.,
תִּמְחֶה אֶת זֵכֶר עֲמָלֵק מִתַּחַת הַשָּׁמַיִם וְגוֹמֵר
"you shall blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under the heavens" etc.
From the plain sense of the wording "And it shall be, when He gives rest" etc.,
it appears that the mitzvah of actually blotting out Amalek
applies only in the future to come;
that even in the days of Shlomo,
who was a man of rest
to actually blot out the remembrance of Amalek.
וְגַם בְּשָׁאוּל כְּתִיב [שְׁמוּאֵל א טו, ב]
And with Shaul too, it is written (Shmuel I 15:2),
which was only a command for that time,
and not part of the mitzvah of the Torah;
"I have sinned, for I have transgressed" etc.
שֶׁעָבַר עַל מִצְוַת הַנָּבִיא בְּשֵׁם ה׳.
for he transgressed the command of the prophet given in Hashem's name.
וְאִם כֵּן מַהוּ מִצְוַת הַזְּכִירָה בָּזֶה
If so, what is the mitzvah of remembrance in this
At any rate it would have been enough
to read the passage in Parshas Teitzei,
since the mitzvah is once a year;
and if it is in order to put remembrance before action,
it should have been read on the thirteenth of Adar,
which sometimes falls several days before?
וְגַם יֵשׁ לְהָבִין הַלָּשׁוֹן מִתַּחַת הַשָּׁמַיִם
We must also understand the phrase "from under the heavens":
וְכִי אוּמַּת עֲמָלֵק דָּר תַּחַת הַשָּׁמַיִם
does the nation of Amalek dwell under the heavens
and not on the earth like the other nations?
And it can be said, as we have said,
that Amalek is the beginning of the kelipah
שֶׁהֵם עַל חֲטָאִים מְיוּחָדִים בְּמַעֲשֶׂה בְּפוֹעַל
which are over specific sins in actual deed.
וְעַל כֵּן אִיתָא בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ [חֵלֶק ג קס, א]
Therefore it is stated in the holy Zohar (III 160a)
עַל פָּסוּק עֲמָלֵק יוֹשֵׁב בְּאֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב [בַּמִּדְבָּר יג, כט]
on the verse "Amalek dwells in the land of the Negev" (Bamidbar 13:29):
"This is the evil inclination, the accuser," etc.,
"which is found constantly in the body";
and to this alludes "in the land of the Negev,"
that is, even in one who is dried out
הוּא גַּם כֵּן נִכְנָס לְלִבּוֹ לְפַתּוֹתוֹ
he too enters his heart to entice him;
"You have given me the land of the Negev" (Yehoshua 15:19)—
that he is dried out of all good, etc.,
אָדָם שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה בִּלְבַד.
a man who has nothing in him but Torah alone
"going on and journeying toward the Negev,"
for all his occupation and aim was
to be dried out of every foreign desire,
and to return them to holiness;
"and he dwelt in the land of the Negev,"
for his soul was already refined
and dried out of all the desires of this world,
and he had repose in this level.
And the kelipah of Amalek is to make one stumble in subtle ways,
even the soul that refines itself
כְּמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
as we find with David HaMelech, alav hashalom,
"And my heart is slain within me" (Tehillim 109:22),
for he had slain the yetzer hara
[יְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק ט הֲלָכָה ה סז, ב]
וְהִתְנַצֵּל הֵן בְּעָווֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי [תְּהִלִּים נא, ז]
and he pleaded, "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity" (Tehillim 51:7)—
שֶׁהָיָה בְּיִשַׁי שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ
which was in Yishai, who died only through the counsel of the serpent
that is, that he had some intention
for his own pleasure in a permitted act,
שֶׁזֶּה נִצְמָח מִפְּגַם הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁל הַנָּחָשׁ.
which grows out of the first blemish of the serpent.
"And in sin did my mother conceive me" (Tehillim ibid.)—
meaning the sin of the impurity of niddah
which is also the blemish of the serpent,
and this is the main power of Amalek
And so we find with Yaavetz,
as it is written (Divrei HaYamim I 4:9),
"And his mother called his name Yaavetz,
saying, 'For I bore him in sorrow'";
שֶׁהָיְתָה מַרְגֶּשֶׁת שֶׁהָיָה לָהּ הָעֶצֶב בְּהַפְלָגָה
for she felt that she had the sorrow to an extraordinary degree,
וּמִזֶּה הִרְגִּישָׁה שֶׁיִּוָּלֵד נֶפֶשׁ יְקָרָה כָּזוֹ
and from this she sensed that so precious a soul would be born,
that the serpent was striving to trip him up through sadness;
and therefore she called him Yaavetz,
to turn the sorrow into good;
for on account of this he was called Yaavetz,
because he counseled and spread Torah in Yisrael
and he restored through his pilpul
הַהֲלָכוֹת שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּכְּחוּ בִּימֵי אֶבְלוֹ שֶׁל מֹשֶׁה
the halachos that were forgotten in the days of mourning for Moshe;
וְהוּא עִיקַּר כֹּחַ תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה
and this is the essential power of Torah she'b'al peh,
which is bound at the root, in Atika;
"Know it, for a great man states a matter
וּמִתְאַמְרָא הֲלָכָה לְמֹשֶׁה מִסִּינַי כְּוָותֵיהּ כּוּלֵּי
and a halachah given to Moshe at Sinai is stated in accordance with him," etc.,
That is, through the reasons of Torah
one reaches up to the root,
and this specifically is the power
to subdue the beginning of the kelipah of Amalek,
which opposes this, as mentioned above.
And as we heard from our holy Rebbe,
זֵכֶר צַדִּיק וְקָדוֹשׁ לִבְרָכָה לְחַיֵּי הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
may the memory of the righteous and holy one be for a blessing, for the life of the World to Come,
עַל פָּסוּק רִפְאוּת תְּהִי לְשָׁרֶּךָ [מִשְׁלֵי ג, ח]
on the verse "It shall be healing to your navel" (Mishlei 3:8):
that words of Torah are a healing
and this is alluded to by the navel,
from which a person is formed.
And regarding Yaavetz, about whom it says,
"You have given me the land of the Negev" etc.—
אָדָם שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ אֶלָּא תּוֹרָה בִּלְבַד
a man who has nothing in him but Torah alone—
שֶׁהִתְפַּלֵּל לְבִלְתִּי עׇצְבִּי [דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א ד, י]
that he prayed "that it not grieve me" (Divrei HaYamim I 4:10):
that the yetzer hara not overpower me and keep me from reviewing;
כִּי זֶהוּ דַּיְיקָא כֹּחוֹ שֶׁל עֲמָלֵק
for this precisely is the power of Amalek,
to cast a person into sadness;
that he cooled you and chilled you.
וּבָזֶה יוּבַן מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בִּפְסִיקְתָּא רַבָּתִי
With this we can understand what they said in Pesikta Rabbasi
מָשָׁל לְמֶלֶךְ שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ פַּרְדֵּס כּוּלֵּי
"A parable of a king who had an orchard," etc.;
to steal from within the orchard;
the dog rose up and bit him.
When the king wished to remind
that he had wanted to steal," etc.,
אוֹמֵר לוֹ זְכוֹר מַה שֶּׁעָשָׂה לְךָ
"he would say to him, 'Remember what was done to you
So too, Yisrael sinned at Refidim
and immediately the dog came and bit them—
to remind Yisrael of the sin
אוֹמֵר זְכוּרִים אַתֶּם לְאוֹתוֹ עֲמָלֵק כּוּלֵּי.
And we raised a difficulty on this:
is there not a greater sin than this,
which the verse mentions explicitly, "Remember" etc.,
אֵת אֲשֶׁר הִקְצַפְתָּ אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ בַּמִּדְבָּר
"how you angered Hashem your God in the wilderness"
However, since this is the power of Amalek,
to bring a person into sadness,
עַל כֵּן אֵין לְהַזְכִּיר הַחֵטְא בְּפֵירוּשׁ
therefore the sin is not to be mentioned explicitly,
כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יִפּוֹל בְּעַצְבוּת מִזֶּה עַצְמוֹ.
so that he not fall into sadness from this very thing.
And also because his power is to make stumble
גַּם מִי שֶׁלִּבּוֹ מְזוּכָּךְ מִכֹּל וָכֹל
even one whose heart is completely refined,
and this is a great shame,
"as the shame of a thief when he is found";
and this is the wording they used
And since this is the essence of the kelipah of Amalek—
which is found in every soul
by force of the first blemish of the serpent—
וְזֶה בֶּאֱמֶת אֵין אוֹפֶן לִמְחוֹק מִכֹּל וָכֹל
and this in truth there is no way to erase completely
when the rectification of the serpent's blemish will be complete;
וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר וְהָיָה בְּהָנִיחַ וְגוֹמֵר
and about this it says, "And it shall be, when He gives rest" etc.,
That is, in the future to come you will merit
to blot out his remembrance completely.
to blot out from his heart whatever is within his ability,
כִּי זֶהוּ עִיקַּר עֵסֶק הָאָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה.
for this is a person's main occupation in this world.
And the time suited for this
הוּא דַּיְיקָא בְּשַׁבָּת זֶה הַסָּמוּךְ לְפוּרִים
is specifically this Shabbos, close to Purim;
and at Shacharis, at the time of the revelation of the aspect of Atika,
the side of the kelipah of Amalek,
which opposes the beginning of holiness.
And this is why it says,
תִּמְחֶה אֶת זֵכֶר עֲמָלֵק מִתַּחַת הַשָּׁמַיִם
"You shall blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under the heavens,"
along the lines of what they said (Sukkah 5a):
וְלֹא עָלוּ מֹשֶׁה וְאֵלִיָּהוּ לַמָּרוֹם כּוּלֵּי
"did Moshe and Eliyahu ascend on high," etc.;
"but is it not written," etc.—"below ten";
דִּכְתִיב [תְּהִלִּים קטו, טז] הַשָּׁמַיִם שָׁמַיִם לַה׳
as it is written (Tehillim 115:16), "The heavens are the heavens of Hashem,
Only the air between heaven and earth,
is within the power of the human soul to reach.
And correspondingly, on the opposing side,
is from the aspect of Amalek,
which is the beginning of kelipah.
Therefore his dwelling is under the heavens,
to prevent the beginning of the bond with the root;
תִּמְחֶה אֶת זֵכֶר עֲמָלֵק מִתַּחַת הַשָּׁמַיִם דַּיְיקָא:
"You shall blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under the heavens"—specifically.

paragraphs.text: I Chronicles 22:9 — “Behold, a son will be born to you; he will be a man of rest. I will grant him rest from all his enemies around him, for Solomon will be his name, and I will grant peace and quiet to Israel in his days.” David’s account of Solomon supplies the language of rest against which Rav Tzadok raises his question.

paragraphs.text: I Samuel 15:24 — “Saul said to Samuel: I have sinned, for I have transgressed the command of the Lord and your words, because I feared the people and listened to their voice.” Rav Tzadok emphasizes “your words” as the prophetic command in that particular hour. This is his interpretive argument within the maamar; the verse itself joins the Lord’s command and Samuel’s words.

paragraphs.text: Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 9:5:8 — “Our father Abraham made the evil inclination good, as it is written, ‘You found his heart faithful before You.’ ... But David could not withstand it and killed it in his heart. What is the reason? ‘My heart is slain within me.’” The contrast between transforming and slaying the inclination is explicit.

paragraphs.text: Bava Batra 17a:6 — “The Sages taught: Four died through the serpent’s counsel: Benjamin son of Jacob, Amram father of Moses, Jesse father of David, and Chileab son of David. All are known through received tradition except Jesse father of David, concerning whom Scripture explains it. ... Was Abigail a daughter of Nahash? Was she not a daughter of Jesse? Rather, she was the daughter of one who died through the serpent’s counsel.” The expression attributes their mortality to the original serpent rather than to personal transgression. Rav Tzadok examines what remains of that primordial damage even in a righteous ancestry.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Tzidkas HaTzaddik 244 — “All of David’s toil all his days was to be saved from alien thoughts, which surrounded him from birth… though he truly slew the evil inclination, it was not entirely cleansed in his days.” Rav Tzadok there explains why the inborn flaw resists full erasure: the inclination of desire cannot be slain, since it is needed for the world and for passion for Torah.

paragraphs.text: Temurah 16a:14–16 — “It was taught: He is Othniel, he is Jabez. What was his name? Judah, the brother of Shimon, was his name. ‘Othniel’—God answered him; ‘Jabez’—he counseled and spread Torah in Israel.” The final phrase of the prayer is explicitly interpreted as protection against the inclination’s interference with Torah study.

paragraphs.text: Bava Batra 12b:2 — “Rav Ashi said: Know that this is so, for a great man says a teaching, and a law received by Moses at Sinai is stated in accordance with him. Perhaps he is like a blind man finding an opening? But does he not give a reason?” The sage’s reasoned understanding can coincide with a received Sinaitic law. Rav Tzadok reads this concurrence as reaching the root beyond ordinary apprehension.

paragraphs.text: Proverbs 3:8 — “It will be healing for your navel, and refreshment for your bones.” The preceding verse calls for fearing the Lord and turning from evil. Rav Tzadok records his teacher’s oral interpretation of the navel as the point of formation and of Torah as healing an inherited deficiency; no separate written attribution is supplied here.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Shemos 5 — “The kelipah of Amalek, of whom it is written ‘asher karcha,’ casts laziness and coldness, and this causes sadness and neglect of Torah, as in ‘l’vilti otzbi.’” Rav Tzadok there reads Yaavetz’s prayer the same way. He adds the antidote: the alacrity of the Avos, rooted in Avraham, which is drawn on at the Shabbos morning meal of Atika and nullifies Amalek’s kelipah.

paragraphs.text: Pesikta Rabbati 12, parable of the orchard and dog — “Rabbi Berekhiah said: To what may this be compared? To a king who had an orchard and a dog sitting and guarding the orchard. The son of the king’s beloved friend came to steal from the orchard. That dog stood up and bit him. When the king wished to remind the son of his beloved friend, without mentioning that he had wished to steal from his orchard, he would say to him: Remember what that dog did to you. So Israel sinned at Rephidim and said, ‘Is the Lord in our midst?’ Immediately the dog came and bit them—this was Amalek.” The parable allows the offense to be recalled through its consequence. Rav Tzadok develops why this form of remembrance is appropriate to a subtle inward failure.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: R. Shneur Zalman of Liadi, Tanya, Likkutei Amarim, ch. 26, concluding paragraphs — “If sadness and anxiety about spiritual matters fall upon a person in the midst of his business, this is recognizably a device of the inclination, intended to cast him afterward into desires. Even concern about grave sins requires appointed times and a fitting occasion, with a settled mind, to contemplate the greatness of Hashem against whom he sinned and attain true contrition. Immediately after his heart has been broken at those appointed times, he should remove sadness completely and believe fully that Hashem has removed his sin and abundantly forgives.”

paragraphs.text: Connection: This distinguishes repentance from the disabling sadness that can imitate it. Rav Tzadok’s indirect reminder of the sin prevents the recollection itself from strengthening Amalek; Tanya supplies the practical distinction between such intrusive guilt and deliberate, restorative repentance.

Rather, I will tell them the episode of Amalek, and they will understand what is written before it.” The retrieved wording is “expose their faces,” where the manuscript cites “whiten their faces.” The source’s concern is the public shame caused by direct accusation.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Machshavos Charutz 5 — “The war is in the heart of man… Hashem’s help is His war against Amalek, clothed in the heart of man… and all of a person’s effort in this is only through remembering.” Rav Tzadok there also reads “when He gives you rest” inwardly, as the calm of a heart no longer troubled by fantasies. At that point one erases Amalek “from every chamber of his mind and heart,” which is the work this world allows.

paragraphs.text: Sukkah 5a:1–4 — “Rabbi Yose says: The Divine Presence never descended below, and Moses and Elijah never ascended to the height, as it is said, ‘The heavens are the Lord’s heavens, but the earth He gave to human beings.’ ... Is it not written, ‘Moses ascended to God’? Below ten handbreadths. Is it not written, ‘Elijah ascended in the storm to heaven’? Below ten handbreadths. ... Nevertheless, does it not say, ‘He holds the face of the throne’? The throne extended downward to ten, and he took hold of it.” The Talmud discusses the boundary between the heavenly and earthly domains. Rav Tzadok applies that boundary to the limit of attainable spiritual apprehension.
